sections.title: Mental model — escape the comparison bound deliberately

blocks.md: Contest reality: std::sort's n log n is usually fine; it stops being fine when n·log n × constant collides with brutal TLs or when the PROBLEM ITSELF is about order statistics. Then radix/counting/BIT machinery enters.
**Radix = counting sort per digit, stable so digit order accumulates correctly. LSD low→high for numbers; MSD for strings/tries-adjacent tasks.**

blocks.label: LSD radix over 16-bit digits
blocks.py:
def radix_sort(a):
    for shift in (0, 16):                     # base 2^16: two passes
        count = [0] * 65536
        for x in a: count[(x >> shift) & 0xFFFF] += 1
        total = 0
        for i in range(65536):
            count[i], total = total, total + count[i]   # positions
        tmp = [0] * len(a)
        for x in a:                           # backwards = STABLE
            d = (x >> shift) & 0xFFFF
            tmp[count[d]] = x; count[d] += 1
        a = tmp
    return a

chain.q: Three inversion-count implementations — when does each win?
chain.a: Merge-count: no deps, cache-friendly, doubles as D&C template. BIT+compression: online/streaming variants, generalizes to distinct-range queries. pb_ds ordered_set: fastest to TYPE in contest; GCC-only. Know all three sentences cold.

chain.q: When do you hand-roll sort instead of std::sort?
chain.a: Radix when n ≥ ~10⁶ AND keys ≤ 10⁹ (2 passes beat comparisons ~3×). Counting when range tiny. Custom merge when inversion/adjacent stats needed anyway. Otherwise NEVER — std::sort is brutally tuned.
Tie-chain strictly: `if (a.k != b.k) return a.k < b.k; return tiebreak(a,b);` Never `<=`; test equal-key floods before submitting — hacked comparators are RE (runtime error) farms.

chain.q: Sorting pairs by second element fast?
chain.a: `sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [&](auto&a, auto&b){ return a.second < b.second; })` or store inverted pairs and rely on default pair-ordering — zero-comparator trick keeps code short under pressure.
